title: Rewards Program (Trend Coins)
problem: M3 retention was weak — users were making one or two purchases and dropping off. The product had no ongoing engagement mechanism between purchase cycles, and the brand was over-reliant on discounts to drive repeat orders.
goals: Improve M3 retention by building a habit-forming engagement loop
Reduce discount dependence by creating non-discount value for repeat users
Boost prepaid adoption by making rewards tangible at checkout
my_role: End-to-end ownership — from ideation and competitor benchmarking through incentive design, A/B test design, and post-launch iteration. Partnered with design and engineering for execution.
key_decisions: Chose a unified coin currency (₹0.10 per coin) over a tier system — simpler to understand, faster to drive habit
Included non-transactional earning (reviews, profile completion) to build engagement between orders, not just at purchase
Made coin balance visible across navigation, checkout, and success screens — visibility drives usage
Ran a randomised A/B test to isolate the program's causal impact from seasonal and campaign noise
execution: Benchmarked loyalty programs across D2C, fashion, and fintech to identify what resonates with Gen Z
Designed coin earning logic, redemption flow, and visibility across key UI touchpoints
A/B tested rewards-enrolled vs control cohort to measure isolated retention lift
Tracked rewards tab views and enrollment rate as leading indicators for M3 retention

metrics.primary: 8% M3 retention lift — A/B validated, causally isolated to the rewards program
metrics.important_note: Overall retention improved ~22% during this period, but that includes seasonal and campaign effects. The 8% is the number attributable specifically to the rewards program.
metrics.leading_indicators: Rewards tab views and coin enrollment rate — validated as predictive of M3 retention
metrics.secondary: Positive shifts in prepaid adoption and AOV among rewards-enrolled users

impact: The rewards program delivered an 8% lift in M3 retention (A/B isolated), turning a discount-first acquisition loop into a loyalty engine. Non-transactional earning created product touchpoints between orders, reducing churn without increasing CAC.
learnings: Isolate causal impact via A/B test — blended metrics (22%) are misleading and hard to defend in reviews
Non-transactional earning builds habit; transactional earning alone just moves the discount
Coin visibility at checkout directly influences redemption and AOV — placement is as important as incentive design

title: Day 0 Offer Strategy — New User Conversion
problem: New users were landing on the app but not converting on their first session. Flat welcome discounts weren't creating urgency and were eroding contribution margin without proportional conversion lift.
goals: Improve Day 0 conversion rate for new users
Create urgency without blanket discount depth
Protect contribution margin while improving conversion
my_role: Owned the offer strategy end-to-end — hypothesis design, cohort structure, A/B test setup, and post-experiment iteration.
key_decisions: Switched from flat discount to escalating cohort model: 15% → 20% → 25% triggered by session count and time elapsed
Added urgency windows — offers expired within defined time to prevent deferral
Set minimum order value floors to protect CM2 even at peak discount depth
execution: Defined cohort logic (session-wise and time-based triggers) with engineering
A/B tested escalating offer vs flat discount control on new user cohorts
Tracked Day 0 CVR, overall new-user CVR, and CM2 per cohort as success metrics

metrics.cm_impact: Contribution margin protected via MOV floors despite higher peak discount depth

impact: The cohort-based escalating offer strategy improved Day 0 conversion by ~10% and overall new-user conversion by ~5%, without sacrificing contribution margin.
learnings: Urgency (time-bound, escalating) outperforms discount depth on Day 0
Flat discounts are blunt instruments — cohort-level personalisation is more efficient
Always pair conversion experiments with a CM guardrail metric

title: Referral Program
problem: NewMe was heavily dependent on paid acquisition. There was no organic or word-of-mouth growth loop. CAC was high and not reducing with scale.
goals: Build a scalable organic acquisition channel
Reduce blended CAC via referral-driven signups
Acquire high-intent users who convert and retain
my_role: Owned end-to-end — incentive design, eligibility rules, flow definition, tracking setup, and post-launch iteration.
key_decisions: Two-sided reward: referrer gets cash incentive, referee gets discount — both sides motivated
Rewards trigger only on first completed order, not signup — ensures quality acquisition not vanity signups
Single share link with upfront reward visibility — simplicity maximises sharing
execution: Designed referral flows across app entry points and post-purchase moments (high-intent sharing windows)
Defined reward logic, eligibility rules, fraud guardrails, and success conditions
Worked with engineering on referral tracking and reward fulfillment
Monitored referral-attributed signups, first-order CVR, and CM2 post-reward cost

metrics.cm_impact: Positive CM2 after referral reward cost — net positive acquisition

impact: The referral program added +12% signups and +3% daily orders with positive CM2 impact, creating a scalable organic channel that reduced dependence on paid acquisition.
learnings: Tie rewards to first order, not signup — quality of referred users is what matters
Two-sided incentives are necessary — single-sided referral programs have low participation
Post-purchase is the highest-intent moment to prompt sharing — that's where we saw most referral initiations

title: POS & Inventory Management System (0→1)
problem: As NewMe expanded into offline retail, stores were running on expensive third-party POS tools with no integration to central inventory. This created ₹50L+ in annual recurring licensing costs, poor inventory visibility, planning inefficiencies, and stockout/overstock cycles that hurt store margins.
goals: Eliminate third-party tool dependency and associated costs
Give store managers real-time inventory visibility
Build a foundation for scalable offline retail expansion
my_role: End-to-end ownership from discovery through rollout. Visited stores pre-discovery, wrote PRD, defined user flows, and led store onboarding and training.
discovery: Before writing a single requirement, I visited stores and observed actual workflows — how staff billed customers, how they tracked inventory, where they made errors. This revealed requirements that no stakeholder had articulated: billing speed under peak load, offline fallback when internet dropped, and the need for a daily stock reconciliation view. The product was shaped by what I saw, not what I was told.
key_decisions: Build in-house vs buy — chose in-house to remove third-party dependency permanently and own the roadmap
Prioritised billing accuracy and inventory consistency in v1 over feature breadth — reliability matters more than richness in operational tools
Designed for store staff, not tech users — minimal cognitive load, optimised for speed under pressure
Built offline fallback mode — stores can't stop billing when internet drops
execution: Conducted store visits and shadowed billing and inventory workflows before PRD
Defined end-to-end requirements for billing, inventory updates, returns, exchanges, and daily reconciliation
Collaborated with engineering on architecture — co-designed with eng lead based on store visit learnings
Led store onboarding: trained staff, ran parallel runs before cutover, managed change resistance

metrics.scale: Rolled out across all offline retail locations

impact: Built an end-to-end POS and inventory system from zero that eliminated ₹50L+ in annual costs, improved planning efficiency by 30%+, and improved store margins by ~3%. Became the operational backbone for NewMe's offline retail expansion.
learnings: Go to the source — store visits revealed requirements no stakeholder meeting would have surfaced
Operational products need radical simplicity — the user is a store staff member under peak load, not a power user
Change management is as hard as the product build — adoption requires training, parallel runs, and patience
0→1 platform work requires co-designing with engineering from day one, not handing over a spec

title: Post-Purchase CX & Support Automation
problem: Query resolution rate was stuck at 20% — 80% of support queries required human intervention. Return approvals were fully agent-dependent with no risk logic, creating high ops cost and abuse exposure. CSAT was 2.5 and return-specific CSAT was 1.0 — effectively one star.
goals: Increase query resolution rate through automation
Improve CSAT across support and returns touchpoints
Reduce agent load without increasing abuse risk
my_role: Led the full initiative — from bot selection and integration to risk-profiling model design, working across product, engineering, support ops, and risk ops.
key_decisions: Implemented Kapture as the bot and ticketing platform — evaluated for automation capability and integration fit
Built a risk-profile model for return approvals: auto-approve 60–65% of users classified as low-risk, human review for flagged profiles
Backtested the risk model at 95% agent approval rate before going live — gave risk ops confidence to sign off
Kept agents focused on complex and flagged cases only — improved both agent efficiency and resolution quality
execution: Mapped end-to-end post-purchase journeys to identify highest-friction support triggers
Integrated Kapture bot and ticketing system with engineering and support ops
Designed risk-profiling logic, backtested against historical return approvals, aligned with risk ops on thresholds
Set up resolution rate and CSAT as primary metrics with weekly tracking
stakeholder_conflict: Support ops wanted maximum automation to reduce headcount pressure. Risk ops flagged that blanket return automation would expose the business to abuse. I resolved this by proposing the risk-profiling layer — auto-approve low-risk users (backtested at 95% agent approval rate), human review for flagged profiles. Both teams aligned once they saw the backtesting data. Neither got everything they wanted, but both got what they needed.
impact: Resolution rate tripled from 20% to 65%. Overall CSAT improved from 2.5 to 3.6. Return CSAT went from 1.0 to 3.0 — the single biggest CSAT jump in any initiative I ran at NewMe.
learnings: Risk-profiling is the unlock for automation at scale — blanket automation creates abuse, selective automation creates trust
Post-purchase is where brand perception is won or lost — a 1.0 return CSAT is a brand emergency, not an ops problem
Backtesting before go-live is how you get risk stakeholders on board — show them data, not arguments
